statement: If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.
heath_proof: For from the even number AB let the even number BC be subtracted: I say that the remainder CA is even. For, since AB is even, it has a half part. [VII. Def. 6] For the same reason BC also has a half part; so that the remainder [CA also has a half part, and]AC is therefore even.

**Statement:** If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

**Step 1.** Let AB be an even number, and let BC, an even number, be subtracted from it. We must show that the remainder AC is even.

**Step 2.** Since AB is even, by Definition D7.6, AB is divisible into two equal parts. That is, there exists a number M such that AB is the sum of M and M, so the dyad (the number 2) measures AB.

**Step 3.** Since BC is even, by Definition D7.6, BC is divisible into two equal parts. That is, there exists a number N such that BC is the sum of N and N, so the dyad measures BC.

**Step 4.** Now AB is composed of BC and the remainder AC. Since the dyad measures AB, we may write AB as M taken together with M (two equal parts). Since the dyad measures BC, we may write BC as N taken together with N (two equal parts).

**Step 5.** Since AB equals BC together with AC, and AB equals M together with M, and BC equals N together with N, we have that M together with M equals N together with N together with AC. By Common Notion CN3 (if equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal), subtracting N from M on one side and N from one of the equal halves on the other, the remainder AC equals (M minus N) taken together with (M minus N). That is, AC is composed of two equal parts, each equal to M minus N.

**Step 6.** Since AC is divisible into two equal parts, AC is even by Definition D7.6. Therefore, if from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder is even. Q.E.D.
